c.tagline: The Karakoram Highway's mountain crossroads, where three of the world's great ranges meet
langs: English (limited, more common with tour operators)

card: Cash is essential — cards are rarely accepted outside a handful of upscale hotels in Gilgit town. Bring enough PKR cash for your whole stay; ATMs exist in town but can be unreliable, especially further into the mountains.
rides: hotel-arranged drivers for Karakoram Highway trips

taxi.color: no standard livery — mostly private sedans and jeeps
taxi.fare: Roughly $1-3 within town; day-long jeep hire for outlying valleys runs $30-60
taxi.fareNote: Fares are negotiated upfront; a 4x4 with driver is essential for reaching Naltar, Rakaposhi viewpoints, and other side valleys

emergency.medical: 1122 (Rescue service, where available); District Headquarters Hospital Gilgit
emergency.note: Serious trauma cases are often referred to Islamabad; travel insurance with medevac coverage is strongly recommended given the remote terrain

religion: Islam (Sunni, Shia, and Ismaili communities, reflecting Gilgit-Baltistan's religious diversity)
walk: Gilgit town's bazaar area is walkable, but the city is a transit hub rather than a stroll-around destination — most travelers pass through en route to Hunza, Skardu, or the Karakoram Highway's mountain valleys, which require a jeep or private car.

safety.safety: Gilgit-Baltistan overall has a strong safety reputation among Pakistan's regions and is popular with independent trekkers and backpackers; exercise normal precautions and check current travel advisories before visiting
safety.crime: Violent crime against tourists is rare; the region's remoteness and mountain terrain (road conditions, altitude, landslides) are bigger practical concerns than crime

hood_landmark.Gilgit Bazaar: Gilgit's main bazaar and Chinar Bagh park
hood_landmark.Konodas: The Gilgit River bank along River View Road

avoid.reason: Northern areas welcoming to tourists, but some routes near the Afghan border need care; check advisories

hood_desc: The commercial heart of Gilgit, with the main bazaar, budget hotels, and travel agents arranging onward trips to Hunza, Skardu, and the Karakoram Highway.

A quiet residential suburb strung along Shahrah-e-Quaid-e-Azam about 4 km southeast of the bazaar, where Gilgit's largest hotels sit. It is the end of town nearest the general bus stand and the road out toward Skardu.

The eastern edge of Gilgit town, about 2 km beyond the bazaar where Nomal Road and River View Road run beside the Gilgit River. A quieter riverside strip, and the way out north toward Nomal and the Naltar valley.

water.note: Drink bottled, boiled or filtered water; glacial tap and stream water is untreated.

transit.sys: No formal public transit; shared Suzuki vans run fixed routes within town
transit.map: No formal transit map; ask your hotel for van routes
transit.note: Most travelers hire a private jeep or join a tour van for onward travel along the Karakoram Highway

transport.air: Gilgit Airport (GIL) has flights from Islamabad (weather-permitting, often delayed or cancelled due to mountain conditions — one of the most scenic flights in the world when it operates)
transport.train: No rail service anywhere in Gilgit-Baltistan
transport.bus: NATCO and private coaches run the spectacular but long Karakoram Highway (KKH) route from Islamabad/Rawalpindi (about 20-24 hours)
transport.ferry: None — Gilgit is a landlocked mountain town with no ferry service
transport.car: Most independent travelers hire a private jeep or car with driver in Gilgit for onward trips to Hunza, Skardu, and the KKH's mountain valleys; road conditions can be affected by landslides and weather

airport.name: Gilgit Airport
airport.distance: ~2 km (10 min) from Gilgit town center
airport.transport: Taxi or hotel pickup; flights are weather-dependent and frequently delayed, so build flexibility into your itinerary

net.m: SCOM (Special Communications Organization) and Zong provide the most reliable coverage in Gilgit-Baltistan; other national carriers have patchy service
net.w: Wifi is available in hotels in Gilgit town but slow and unreliable further into the valleys
net.gb: ~$3-6 for a prepaid SIM with a few GB
net.fwn: Some social media and VOIP services face intermittent restrictions in Pakistan; a VPN can help but isn't always necessary
net.ap: A local SCOM or Zong SIM (best coverage in the mountains) is recommended, purchased with your passport in Islamabad or Gilgit

tip.s: Tipping (baksheesh) is customary for guides, drivers, and porters — 10% or a fixed daily amount is appreciated
tip.r: Rounding up or leaving 10% is welcomed at restaurants, though not obligatory

landmarks: Kargah Buddha
A serene 7th-century Buddha carved high on a cliff face in Kargah Nala, silent witness to Gilgit's centuries as a Silk Road Buddhist crossroads.
Raja Bazaar (Gilgit Bazaar)
The town's bustling commercial artery, where traders from Hunza, Baltistan and Xinjiang haggle over dried apricots, gemstones, pattu wool and Chinese goods.
Danyor Suspension Bridge
A rattling 1960s wooden-planked bridge slung dramatically across the Gilgit River, long one of Pakistan's most photogenic and nerve-testing crossings.
Chinar Bagh
Gilgit's riverside garden of giant plane trees shelters memorials to the 1947 liberation and offers cool evening strolls along the rushing grey river.
Chinese Memorial (Danyor Cemetery)
A quiet walled cemetery honoring Chinese workers who died building the Karakoram Highway, a moving monument to the mountain road's human cost.
Jaglot Three Mountain Ranges Junction
A short drive south, a viewpoint marks the meeting of the Karakoram, Himalaya and Hindu Kush ranges at the confluence of the Indus and Gilgit rivers.
Naltar Valley
A day-trippable alpine valley of pine forests, ski slopes and the jewel-colored Naltar Lakes, whose blues and greens seem almost unreal.
Rakaposhi Viewpoint
On the Karakoram Highway toward Hunza, roadside terraces serve tea beneath the stupendous 5,800-metre ice face of 7,788-metre Rakaposhi.
Henzal Stupa
The weathered remains of an ancient Buddhist stupa west of town, evidence of the sacred geography that once lined the Gilgit valley.
Gilgit River Confluence Walks
Trails and bridges around town frame the milky-jade Gilgit and Hunza rivers churning between stark ochre mountainsides dotted with poplar-green villages.

train.note: There is no railway in Gilgit-Baltistan - Pakistan Railways' network (https://www.pakrail.gov.pk/) stops far to the south at Havelian near Abbottabad. All travel here is on the Karakoram Highway by road, or by the spectacular but frequently weather-cancelled flight from Islamabad.

intl.to: Kashgar (China) - via the Khunjerab Pass, roughly May-Oct
intl.op: NATCO — tickets at the Gilgit NATCO terminal, no online booking

bus.note: The Khunjerab Pass at 4,693 m is the highest paved border crossing in the world and is open only in the summer season, roughly May to October, with a Chinese visa required in advance. NATCO's bus goes via Sost, where Pakistani exit formalities are done. Domestically, NATCO and private coaches run down the Karakoram Highway to Islamabad in 16-20 hours and up to Hunza and Skardu; landslides can close the road for days.

ferry.note: Gilgit is high in the Karakoram with no navigable water, so there are no ferries. Attabad Lake in Hunza, formed by a 2010 landslide, once required boat crossings but is now bypassed by tunnels.

full.name: Hunza Valley & Karimabad
full.blurb: Terraced valley of apricot orchards below the Karakoram peaks, centered on the old royal town of Karimabad.

full.name: Attabad Lake
full.blurb: Turquoise lake formed by a 2010 landslide that dammed the Hunza River, now toured by boat between cliffs.
